court: Office of Hearings and Appeals — Director's Decisions (U.S. Dept. of the Interior)
title: 16 OHA 115 — IN RE MILLARD
text:
IN THE MATTER OF ROBERT L. AND
ERMA P. MILLARD
D-98-54 Decided July 28, 1998
Appeal from a decision of the Yuma, Arizona, Field Office, Bureau of Land
Management, terminating residential occupancy permit on Federal lands. CAAZCA 23502.
Affirmed.
1. Cabin Sites: Public Conservation and Recreation Areas
BLM properly terminates a permit for a private residence site on
public land on the lower Colorado River where the permit provided
for a year to year occupancy and was subject to termination on
notice at the end of any year's period, and where BLM's land use
planning showed that the public interest would be best served by
opening the area to public recreational access.
APPEARANCES: Robert and Erma Millard, pro sese; Richard R. Greenfield, Esq., Office of
the Field Solicitor, U. S. Department of the Interior, Phoenix, Arizona, for the Bureau of
Land Management.
OPINION BY WOLFGANG E. NEUDORFER
Robert and Erma Millard (Appellants) have appealed from a February 5, 1998 decision
of the Yuma, Arizona, Field Office, Bureau of Land Management (BLM), providing notice of
termination, and terminating their residential occupancy permit CAAZCA 23502 effective
December 31, 1998. Appellants have also petitioned for a stay pending a decision on appeal.
The land covered by the permit is Parcel WC-23, consisting of 0.19 acres 15 miles south of
Palo Verde, Imperial County, California, on the west bank of the Colorado River.
Background
The BLM's Yuma, Arizona, Field office, formerly the Lower Colorado Land Use
Office, was established in 1961 by Secretarial Order No. 2854 to eliminate trespass
occupancy along the lower Colorado River corridor, on lands withdrawn by the Bureau of
Reclamation. In the 1960's, that office issued residential occupancy permits to temporarily
16 OHA 115

resolve trespass occupancies along the river. The permits legalized trespass occupancies on
Federal land on a year-to-year basis and were subject to termination when other needs for the
land were identified. Thus, the permit issued to Appellants provides at paragraph 5 that it
was to run for successive one-year periods and could be terminated at the end of any such
period "by written notice served by the United States upon the applicant at least ninety (90)
days in advance thereof." The permit further provided, at paragraph 8, that the granting
thereof did not confer "any title to or property interest in any of the lands within the permit
area, nor * * * any right to renew or extend the permit beyond the period provided for in
paragraph 5 hereof." Paragraph 16 provided that all of the rights of the permittee would
cease upon the termination of the permit.
Beginning in the 1960's the Department developed and implemented various land use
plans for the Colorado River. In 1964, the Lower Colorado River Land Use Plan established
long range proposals for recreational use along the river. In 1975 the La Paz Management
Framework Plan carried forward and expanded earlier planning decisions. This was followed
in 1975 by the Ehrenberg-Cibola Recreation Management Plan, the Yuma District Resource
Management Plan of 1986, and the Ehrenberg-Cibola Recreation Area Management plan of
1994 (RAMP). The Yuma District Management Plan specifically states that existing
residential permits would be phased out and associated improvements removed. The purpose
of this land use planning was to open the area up for recreational access by the general public.
Over the years, the BLM provided ample notice to permittees that the lands were
needed and that their permits would be terminated. By letters of September 17, 1973, March
6, 1992, February 28, 1995, and September 27, 1996, the BLM provided notice that the
permits would be phased out and invited permittees to participate in the planning process for
the lands. BLM also published notice of its intention to implement the Ehrenberg-Cibola
RAMP. 59 Fed. Reg. 18151 (Apr. 15, 1994).
Arguments of the Parties
The Appellants contend that BLM has no explicit reason for terminating the permits,
and that there are no tangible or formal concrete plans for the construction of improvements
to require the termination of their permit. Appellants note that under the original permitting
scheme, permits were to be granted until there was another specific use for the property.
Appellants contend that no specific other use for the property is contemplated.
The Appellants refer to the Ehrenberg-Cibola RAMP noting that it outlines a plan for a
recreational facility including a fishing pier and a parking lot embracing the their permit area.
Appellants assert that there are no plans to construct this facility, only vague future
possibilities.
The Appellants recite that oral inquiries made of employees of various agencies,
including the Fish and Wildlife Service, revealed a lack of knowledge, on the part of these
16 OHA 116

employees, as to plans for the recreational development outlined in the RAMP. Appellants
note that the RAMP does not specifically indicate that their permit area will actually interfere
with thed parking lot and fishing pier. Appellants contend that there is little use of the area
by recreationists and that expansion is unnecessary.
The Appellants request that BLM continue to extend their permit until the land they
occupy will be used for a specific purpose at a specific time.
The BLM 1/ points out the limitations of the permits under which Appellants occupy
the site. BLM asserts that termination of the permit, with ample notice, is fully consistent
with BLM's responsibility for managing the public lands as exercised in the development of
the various land management plans covering the area.
Counsel for BLM has submitted the affidavit of Joy Gilbert, a senior technical
specialist in the Yuma Field Office, who manages the special permitting program on the
lower Colorado River corridor. Gilbert states in her affidavit that the Millards' permit site is
one of the few remaining private permits, is in a prime waterfront recreation use area and is
inconsistent with opening the area for use by the public (Id., at 4.)
Gilbert further states that BLM plans to install a fishing pier at the site of the
residential permits at Walter's Camp (the area in which the Millards' site is located), and that
plans for the site are set forth in the Ehrenberg-Cibola RAMP (Id., at 8, 9.)
Counsel for BLM concludes that terminating the Millards' permit was a proper use of
BLM's discretionary authority and that the Millards have shown no error of fact or law in the
BLM determination.
Discussion
[1] The Ehrenberg-Cibola RAMP covers a special recreation management area
embracing approximately 209,410 acres of land along the Colorado River in western Arizona
and southeastern California. BLM administers 114,050 acres of this land. The objective of
the RAMP is to “provide the public with a broad base of recreational activities within an
enjoyable recreational setting * * * to enhance the facilities and services through improved
__________________________
1/ Counsel for BLM asserts in his answer that neither the Millard's notice of appeal nor their
statement of reasons was served on his Phoenix, Arizona, office. The regulations pertaining
to ad hoc appeals provide for the mailing, by an appellant, of a notice of appeal and statement
of reasons "to the Departmental official whose action or decision is being appealed." The
Millards' notice of appeal and statement of reasons indicate that copies were served on the
BLM's Yuma Field Office. 43 C.F.R. § 4.701.
16 OHA 117

facility design, development of interpretive areas, brochures and maps, and increased Bureau
of Land Management (BLM) presence.” (RAMP at 1.)
The RAMP states that the Walter's Camp area was identified by the public during
scoping meetings "as an ideal location for a fishing pier." The planning goal is to “[p]rovide
a universally accessible facility for all users to access the waters of the Colorado River for
pier fishing in an area that has limited opportunities for this type of fishing activity.”
The RAMP states that the "Concept" is to develop a public recreational facility which
will meet all accessibility criteria and will include a parking area and fishing pier (RAMP at
34.)
As noted earlier, notice of the RAMP was published in 59 Fed. Reg. 18151 (Apr. 15,
1994). That notice summarized important aspects of the RAMP and provided a 30-day
appeal period.
Section 102 of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA) 43
U.S.C. § 1701(a)(2) (1994) states that the national interest will be best realized if the present
and future use of the public lands "is projected through a land use planning process
coordinated with other Federal and State planning efforts." Section 202, 43 U.S.C. § 1712,
invests the Secretary with the authority to develop, maintain, and revise land use plans.
A regulation applicable to this appeal, 43 C.F.R. § 21.4 (a)(2), provides:
Whenever the Authorized Officer determines that the public need for use
of a recreation or conservation area has grown to a point where continued private
cabin site use is no longer in the public interest, the procedures set forth in
paragraph (b) of this section will be invoked to phase out existing permits by
reducing and eliminating renewals, or extensions, consistent with protection of
legitimate investment in improvements. [2/]
Having reviewed the Appellants' arguments in light of the above authorities, we
conclude that BLM's determination to terminate the Millards' permit is proper and must be
sustained. Appellants' rights of occupancy are, in the first instance, clearly defined by the
permit itself. That permit circumscribed their occupancy as one from year to year,
specifically excluded title to or property interest in the permitted land, and provided for
termination on notice at the end of such 1-year periods. Furthermore, the terms of the permit
did not oblige the grantor to provide specific reasons for termination or non-renewal. Thus,
__________________________
2/ 43 C.F.R. § 21.4 (b) provides guidelines for protection of investments in improvements.
16 OHA 118

even in absence the extensive justification provided by this record for termination of the
permit, Appellants have no legal or equitable right for its continuance. Therefore, the facts
that, as Appellants argue, neither a time certain nor construction specifications are in place
for the fishing pier or parking lot are not a bar to the BLM's termination of the permit.
Nevertheless, the regulation quoted above does provide that termination of occupancy
sites such as the Millards' should be attended by a determination of the public interest. The
record in this case amply demonstrates that the public interest will best be served by
termination of the private occupancy permits to make way for greater public recreational
opportunities. The weighing of the public interest in public land use determinations is
committed to the sound discretion of the BLM and its experts. As members of the public,
Appellants may participate in BLM's land use planning and may appeal certain planning
decisions. However, their disagreement with such decisions, while understandable, provides
no cause for reversal in the absence of a showing of error.
In administrative proceedings before the Department, the general rule is that there be
proof by a preponderance of the evidence that a decision is in error if an appellant is to
prevail. Bender v. Clark, 744 F.2d 1424 (10th Cir. 1984). Thus, in order to prevail in a
challenge to a BLM decision granting or denying applications to use Federal lands, the
challenging party must demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that the BLM erred
in reaching its conclusion. Appellants have made no such showing and the record herein
supports the BLM's decision.
Therefore, pursuant to the authority delegated to the Ad Hoc Board of Appeals by the
Secretary of the Interior, 43 C.F.R. § 4.1(b)(4), the decision appealed from is affirmed and
the request for stay is denied.
